raw_evidence.label: The hook match: Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde (AET), Miami, 2026-07-03
raw_evidence.content: On the night of 3 July 2026 at Miami Stadium (Hard Rock Stadium under FIFA clean naming), Cape Verde took reigning world champions Argentina to extra time in the World Cup Round of 32 and came within nine minutes of the biggest upset in tournament history. Lionel Messi opened with a sublime touch-and-finish in the 29th minute; Deroy Duarte squeezed a shot into the far corner just before the hour (59') to level; Lisandro Martinez restored Argentina's lead two minutes into extra time (92'); Sidny Lopes Cabral curled in what Sky Sports called 'arguably the goal of the tournament' in the 103rd minute; and the winner, in the 111th, was a Cristian Romero header from a corner that went in off Cape Verde defender Diney Borges — an own-goal deflection, not an Argentine strike. Goalkeeper Vozinha (Cape Verde's 39-year-old captain) made eight saves. Both Cape Verde goalscorers were born in the Netherlands — the diaspora literally scored every Cape Verdean goal of the night. Note for downstream fact-checking: the winning goal is credited as a Diney own goal (Romero's header deflected in), and UK outlets dated the report 4 July (overnight UK time); the match was played 3 July local time in Miami. The dataset's international_results.csv records this match as the extra-time score 3-2.

Method: compute percentage. Result: fitted params (full sample): C=0.6614 B=2.0468 H=0.2965 (home shift = 119 Elo po Code: code/fit_outcome_model.py:L84-118. [full data_table in raw_evidence]

raw_evidence.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
raw_evidence.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_19: what were Cape Verde's chances against Argentina? ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
C, B, H, nll = fit_symmetric(m.x.values, m.home.values, m.y.values)
print(f"fitted params (full sample): C={C:.4f} B={B:.4f} H={H:.4f} "
      f"(home shift = {H * 400:.0f} Elo points; mean NLL {nll:.4f})")
C_, B_, H_ = round(C, 4), round(B, 4), round(H, 4)
print(f"PUBLISHED (rounded, inlined in client_model.js): C={C_} B={B_} H={H_}, SCALE=400")
arg = elo[(elo.date == "2026-07-03") & (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde")].iloc[0]
# ratings rounded to 1 dp -- the SAME values inlined in client_model.js, so the
# browser recomputation agrees with the published numbers by construction
r_arg, r_cpv = round(arg.pre_home, 1), round(arg.pre_away, 1)

raw_evidence.label: Both Cape Verde scorers vs Argentina were born in Rotterdam
raw_evidence.content: The two men who scored against the world champions were both born in the same Dutch port city. Deroy D'Encarnacao Duarte (b. 4 July 1999, Rotterdam — his goal came the night before his 27th birthday) grew up in Sparta Rotterdam's academy from 2006, played 9 times for the Netherlands at U19 level, then accepted a Cape Verde call-up in March 2022; the 59th-minute equaliser against Argentina was his FIRST international goal. His older brother Laros Duarte (b. 1997, also Rotterdam) is in the same World Cup squad. Sidny Lopes Cabral (b. 18 September 2002, Rotterdam) came through FC Twente's youth ranks, was first called up by Cape Verde in 2023 for a friendly against Comoros, and curled in the 103rd-minute equaliser that Sky Sports called arguably the goal of the tournament. Neither scorer was born in Cape Verde; both chose the country of their parents. This is the diaspora thesis in a single scoreline — and it gives the Editor a precise line: every Cape Verdean goal against Argentina was scored by a son of Rotterdam.

raw_evidence.label: The hook match: Argentina 3-2 Cape Verde (AET), Miami, 2026-07-03
raw_evidence.content: On the night of 3 July 2026 at Miami Stadium (Hard Rock Stadium under FIFA clean naming), Cape Verde took reigning world champions Argentina to extra time in the World Cup Round of 32 and came within nine minutes of the biggest upset in tournament history. Lionel Messi opened with a sublime touch-and-finish in the 29th minute; Deroy Duarte squeezed a shot into the far corner just before the hour (59') to level; Lisandro Martinez restored Argentina's lead two minutes into extra time (92'); Sidny Lopes Cabral curled in what Sky Sports called 'arguably the goal of the tournament' in the 103rd minute; and the winner, in the 111th, was a Cristian Romero header from a corner that went in off Cape Verde defender Diney Borges — an own-goal deflection, not an Argentine strike. Goalkeeper Vozinha (Cape Verde's 39-year-old captain) made eight saves. Both Cape Verde goalscorers were born in the Netherlands — the diaspora literally scored every Cape Verdean goal of the night. Note for downstream fact-checking: the winning goal is credited as a Diney own goal (Romero's header deflected in), and UK outlets dated the report 4 July (overnight UK time); the match was played 3 July local time in Miami. The dataset's international_results.csv records this match as the extra-time score 3-2.

raw_evidence.label: The run: first-ever qualification (Oct 2025) and an unbeaten-in-90-minutes World Cup
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde qualified for a World Cup for the first time on 13 October 2025, beating Eswatini 3-0 in Praia to win their CAF qualifying group. At the 2026 tournament they were drawn into Group H with Spain, Uruguay and Saudi Arabia — and never lost a match in 90 minutes all tournament: 0-0 vs Spain (June 15), 2-2 vs Uruguay (June 21, goals from Kevin Pina and Helio Varela), 0-0 vs Saudi Arabia (June 26). Three draws and 3 points were enough to finish second in the group, making Cape Verde the smallest nation ever to reach the knockout stage of a FIFA World Cup. Their exit required the reigning champions, extra time, and an own goal. For the analyst: all of these matches are rows in international_results.csv (scores recorded at full-time/extra-time, no shootouts in these fixtures).

raw_evidence.content: Match by match against the Elo expectations: Cape Verde entered the tournament at 1654 and was given a 3.7% win expectancy against Spain (2219) -- and drew 0-0 (+28 points). Against Uruguay (17.1% expectancy) they came from behind twice to draw 2-2 (+20). The 0-0 with Saudi Arabia was the one dead-even fixture (49.2%). In the Round of 32, Argentina (2225) towered 523 points above them (4.7% expectancy); the 2-3 extra-time defeat cost only 3 rating points. Net: 0 wins, 3 draws, 1 ET loss, group goals 2-2, and +45 Elo across the tournament -- the 'never lost in 90 minutes' record of det_02, quantified.

raw_evidence.label: The run: first-ever qualification (Oct 2025) and an unbeaten-in-90-minutes World Cup
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde qualified for a World Cup for the first time on 13 October 2025, beating Eswatini 3-0 in Praia to win their CAF qualifying group. At the 2026 tournament they were drawn into Group H with Spain, Uruguay and Saudi Arabia — and never lost a match in 90 minutes all tournament: 0-0 vs Spain (June 15), 2-2 vs Uruguay (June 21, goals from Kevin Pina and Helio Varela), 0-0 vs Saudi Arabia (June 26). Three draws and 3 points were enough to finish second in the group, making Cape Verde the smallest nation ever to reach the knockout stage of a FIFA World Cup. Their exit required the reigning champions, extra time, and an own goal. For the analyst: all of these matches are rows in international_results.csv (scores recorded at full-time/extra-time, no shootouts in these fixtures).

raw_evidence.label: The World Cup arc: four matches, never beaten in 90 minutes
raw_evidence.content: Match by match against the Elo expectations: Cape Verde entered the tournament at 1654 and was given a 3.7% win expectancy against Spain (2219) -- and drew 0-0 (+28 points). Against Uruguay (17.1% expectancy) they came from behind twice to draw 2-2 (+20). The 0-0 with Saudi Arabia was the one dead-even fixture (49.2%). In the Round of 32, Argentina (2225) towered 523 points above them (4.7% expectancy); the 2-3 extra-time defeat cost only 3 rating points. Net: 0 wins, 3 draws, 1 ET loss, group goals 2-2, and +45 Elo across the tournament -- the 'never lost in 90 minutes' record of det_02, quantified.

raw_evidence.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
raw_evidence.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_19: what were Cape Verde's chances against Argentina? ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
C, B, H, nll = fit_symmetric(m.x.values, m.home.values, m.y.values)
print(f"fitted params (full sample): C={C:.4f} B={B:.4f} H={H:.4f} "
      f"(home shift = {H * 400:.0f} Elo points; mean NLL {nll:.4f})")
C_, B_, H_ = round(C, 4), round(B, 4), round(H, 4)
print(f"PUBLISHED (rounded, inlined in client_model.js): C={C_} B={B_} H={H_}, SCALE=400")
arg = elo[(elo.date == "2026-07-03") & (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde")].iloc[0]
# ratings rounded to 1 dp -- the SAME values inlined in client_model.js, so the
# browser recomputation agrees with the published numbers by construction
r_arg, r_cpv = round(arg.pre_home, 1), round(arg.pre_away, 1)
print(f"pre-match ratings 2026-07-03 (neutral venue): "
      f"Argentina {r_arg}, Cape Verde {r_cpv} (gap {r_arg - r_cpv:.1f})")
p_loss_cv, p_draw_cv, p_win_cv = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_cpv - r_arg) / 400]), 0)[0]
print(f"model, from Cape Verde's side: win in 90' {p_win_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"level after 90' (reach extra time) {p_draw_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"lose in 90' {p_loss_cv * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"P(advance) if a level match is a coin flip (assumption): "
      f"{(p_win_cv + 0.5 * p_draw_cv) * 100:.1f}%")
# symmetry sanity: identical from Argentina's side
pa = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_arg - r_cpv) / 400]), 0)[0]
assert abs(pa[0] - p_win_cv) < 1e-12 and abs(pa[1] - p_draw_cv) < 1e-12
print("side-swap symmetry check: PASS (neutral venue, listed side irrelevant)")
# the same model across Cape Verde's whole tournament, for the record
for _, r_ in elo[(elo.tournament == "FIFA World Cup") & (elo.date >= "2026-06-01")
                 & ((elo.home_team == "Cape Verde") | (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde"))].iterrows():
    cv_home = r_.home_team == "Cape Verde"
    rcv = round(r_.pre_home if cv_home else r_.pre_away, 1)
    ropp = round(r_.pre_away if cv_home else r_.pre_home, 1)
    pl, pd_, pw = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(rcv - ropp) / 400]), 0)[0]
    res = f"{int(r_.home_score)}-{int(r_.away_score)}"
    opp = r_.away_team if cv_home else r_.home_team
    print(f"  {r_.date} vs {opp} ({res}): P(CV win)={pw * 100:.1f}% "
          f"P(draw)={pd_ * 100:.1f}% P(CV loss)={pl * 100:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
raw_evidence.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_19: what were Cape Verde's chances against Argentina? ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
C, B, H, nll = fit_symmetric(m.x.values, m.home.values, m.y.values)
print(f"fitted params (full sample): C={C:.4f} B={B:.4f} H={H:.4f} "
      f"(home shift = {H * 400:.0f} Elo points; mean NLL {nll:.4f})")
C_, B_, H_ = round(C, 4), round(B, 4), round(H, 4)
print(f"PUBLISHED (rounded, inlined in client_model.js): C={C_} B={B_} H={H_}, SCALE=400")
arg = elo[(elo.date == "2026-07-03") & (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde")].iloc[0]
# ratings rounded to 1 dp -- the SAME values inlined in client_model.js, so the
# browser recomputation agrees with the published numbers by construction
r_arg, r_cpv = round(arg.pre_home, 1), round(arg.pre_away, 1)
print(f"pre-match ratings 2026-07-03 (neutral venue): "
      f"Argentina {r_arg}, Cape Verde {r_cpv} (gap {r_arg - r_cpv:.1f})")
p_loss_cv, p_draw_cv, p_win_cv = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_cpv - r_arg) / 400]), 0)[0]
print(f"model, from Cape Verde's side: win in 90' {p_win_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"level after 90' (reach extra time) {p_draw_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"lose in 90' {p_loss_cv * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"P(advance) if a level match is a coin flip (assumption): "
      f"{(p_win_cv + 0.5 * p_draw_cv) * 100:.1f}%")
# symmetry sanity: identical from Argentina's side
pa = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_arg - r_cpv) / 400]), 0)[0]
assert abs(pa[0] - p_win_cv) < 1e-12 and abs(pa[1] - p_draw_cv) < 1e-12
print("side-swap symmetry check: PASS (neutral venue, listed side irrelevant)")
# the same model across Cape Verde's whole tournament, for the record
for _, r_ in elo[(elo.tournament == "FIFA World Cup") & (elo.date >= "2026-06-01")
                 & ((elo.home_team == "Cape Verde") | (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde"))].iterrows():
    cv_home = r_.home_team == "Cape Verde"
    rcv = round(r_.pre_home if cv_home else r_.pre_away, 1)
    ropp = round(r_.pre_away if cv_home else r_.pre_home, 1)
    pl, pd_, pw = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(rcv - ropp) / 400]), 0)[0]
    res = f"{int(r_.home_score)}-{int(r_.away_score)}"
    opp = r_.away_team if cv_home else r_.home_team
    print(f"  {r_.date} vs {opp} ({res}): P(CV win)={pw * 100:.1f}% "
          f"P(draw)={pd_ * 100:.1f}% P(CV loss)={pl * 100:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
raw_evidence.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_19: what were Cape Verde's chances against Argentina? ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
C, B, H, nll = fit_symmetric(m.x.values, m.home.values, m.y.values)
print(f"fitted params (full sample): C={C:.4f} B={B:.4f} H={H:.4f} "
      f"(home shift = {H * 400:.0f} Elo points; mean NLL {nll:.4f})")
C_, B_, H_ = round(C, 4), round(B, 4), round(H, 4)
print(f"PUBLISHED (rounded, inlined in client_model.js): C={C_} B={B_} H={H_}, SCALE=400")
arg = elo[(elo.date == "2026-07-03") & (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde")].iloc[0]
# ratings rounded to 1 dp -- the SAME values inlined in client_model.js, so the
# browser recomputation agrees with the published numbers by construction
r_arg, r_cpv = round(arg.pre_home, 1), round(arg.pre_away, 1)
print(f"pre-match ratings 2026-07-03 (neutral venue): "
      f"Argentina {r_arg}, Cape Verde {r_cpv} (gap {r_arg - r_cpv:.1f})")
p_loss_cv, p_draw_cv, p_win_cv = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_cpv - r_arg) / 400]), 0)[0]
print(f"model, from Cape Verde's side: win in 90' {p_win_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"level after 90' (reach extra time) {p_draw_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"lose in 90' {p_loss_cv * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"P(advance) if a level match is a coin flip (assumption): "
      f"{(p_win_cv + 0.5 * p_draw_cv) * 100:.1f}%")
# symmetry sanity: identical from Argentina's side
pa = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_arg - r_cpv) / 400]), 0)[0]
assert abs(pa[0] - p_win_cv) < 1e-12 and abs(pa[1] - p_draw_cv) < 1e-12
print("side-swap symmetry check: PASS (neutral venue, listed side irrelevant)")
# the same model across Cape Verde's whole tournament, for the record
for _, r_ in elo[(elo.tournament == "FIFA World Cup") & (elo.date >= "2026-06-01")
                 & ((elo.home_team == "Cape Verde") | (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde"))].iterrows():
    cv_home = r_.home_team == "Cape Verde"
    rcv = round(r_.pre_home if cv_home else r_.pre_away, 1)
    ropp = round(r_.pre_away if cv_home else r_.pre_home, 1)
    pl, pd_, pw = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(rcv - ropp) / 400]), 0)[0]
    res = f"{int(r_.home_score)}-{int(r_.away_score)}"
    opp = r_.away_team if cv_home else r_.home_team
    print(f"  {r_.date} vs {opp} ({res}): P(CV win)={pw * 100:.1f}% "
          f"P(draw)={pd_ * 100:.1f}% P(CV loss)={pl * 100:.1f}%")

Data: 01_diaspora/cape_verde_emigrants_by_destination.csv, 01_diaspora/undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx, 02_remittances/remittances_pct_gdp_tidy.csv, 03_football/international_results.csv, 03_football/squad_2026.csv, 04_population/population_total_tidy.csv, 02_remittances/Metadata_Country_*.csv + 04_population/Metadata_Country_*.csv (aggregate filters).

raw_evidence.label: Validation: the odds model beats naive baselines by 19% out-of-sample
raw_evidence.content: Trained only on 1990-2014 (19,514 matches) and tested on 10,681 fully out-of-sample matches from 2015-2026, the model's 3-class Brier score is 0.5151 vs 0.6346 for a base-rate baseline (18.8% better); log-loss 0.8753 vs 1.0524 (16.8% better). Calibration is tight across all deciles: teams given e.g. a 15.1% win chance won 13.7% of the time, and the maximum predicted-vs-observed gap in any decile is 2.5 points. The underlying Elo expectancy alone scores Brier 0.1284 vs 0.1918 for a coin-flip baseline. LEVEL STATEMENT: this validates PER-MATCH outcome probabilities -- the same level as the ana_19 headline (one match, Cape Verde vs Argentina), so headline and validation match; no tournament-level aggregate is claimed anywhere. What would falsify ana_19: a calibration table where low-probability deciles won far more often than predicted, or a Brier no better than base rates -- neither occurs.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_20: out-of-sample backtest 2015-2026 ---
print("=== ana_20 ===")
train, test = m[m.date < "2015-01-01"], m[m.date >= "2015-01-01"]
Ct, Bt, Ht, nll_tr = fit_symmetric(train.x.values, train.home.values, train.y.values)
print(f"train: {len(train):,} matches (1990-2014), params C={Ct:.4f} B={Bt:.4f} H={Ht:.4f}")
print(f"test : {len(test):,} matches (2015-2026), fully out-of-sample")
p_test = probs(Ct, Bt, Ht, test.x.values, test.home.values)
onehot = np.eye(3)[test.y.values]
brier_model = ((p_test - onehot) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()
base = np.array([(train.y == 0).mean(), (train.y == 1).mean(), (train.y == 2).mean()])
brier_base = ((base - onehot) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()
ll_model = -np.log(np.clip(p_test[np.arange(len(test)), test.y.values], 1e-12, None)).mean()
ll_base = -np.log(base[test.y.values]).mean()
print(f"3-class Brier: model {brier_model:.4f} vs base-rate baseline {brier_base:.4f} "
      f"({(1 - brier_model / brier_base) * 100:.1f}% better)")
print(f"log-loss    : model {ll_model:.4f} vs baseline {ll_base:.4f} "
      f"({(1 - ll_model / ll_base) * 100:.1f}% better)")
# Elo expectancy itself (W in {0,.5,1} vs We), same holdout
we = 1 / (10 ** (-(test.pre_home + 100 * test.home - test.pre_away) / 400) + 1)
w = np.select([test.home_score > test.away_score,
               test.home_score == test.away_score], [1.0, 0.5], 0.0)
print(f"Elo expectancy Brier (W vs We): {((we - w) ** 2).mean():.4f} vs "
      f"constant-0.5 baseline {((0.5 - w) ** 2).mean():.4f}")
# calibration: predicted home-win deciles vs observed home-win rate
dec = pd.DataFrame({"p": p_test[:, 2], "won": (test.y == 2).values})
dec["bin"] = np.clip((dec.p * 10).astype(int), 0, 9)
cal = dec.groupby("bin").agg(n=("won", "size"), pred=("p", "mean"),
                             actual=("won", "mean")).round(3)
print("calibration (predicted home-win prob decile vs observed, test set):")
print(cal.to_string())
gap = (cal.pred - cal.actual).abs().max()
print(f"max |predicted - observed| across bins: {gap:.3f}")
print("LEVEL VALIDATED: per-match outcome probabilities, out-of-sample 2015-2026.")
print("The ana_19 headline (Cape Verde's chance in ONE match vs Argentina) is a")
print("per-match probability at exactly this level; no tournament-level or")
print("multi-match aggregate is claimed or validated.")

raw_evidence.content: Trained only on 1990-2014 (19,514 matches) and tested on 10,681 fully out-of-sample matches from 2015-2026, the model's 3-class Brier score is 0.5151 vs 0.6346 for a base-rate baseline (18.8% better); log-loss 0.8753 vs 1.0524 (16.8% better). Calibration is tight across all deciles: teams given e.g. a 15.1% win chance won 13.7% of the time, and the maximum predicted-vs-observed gap in any decile is 2.5 points. The underlying Elo expectancy alone scores Brier 0.1284 vs 0.1918 for a coin-flip baseline. LEVEL STATEMENT: this validates PER-MATCH outcome probabilities -- the same level as the ana_19 headline (one match, Cape Verde vs Argentina), so headline and validation match; no tournament-level aggregate is claimed anywhere. What would falsify ana_19: a calibration table where low-probability deciles won far more often than predicted, or a Brier no better than base rates -- neither occurs.

# --- ana_20: out-of-sample backtest 2015-2026 ---
print("=== ana_20 ===")
train, test = m[m.date < "2015-01-01"], m[m.date >= "2015-01-01"]
Ct, Bt, Ht, nll_tr = fit_symmetric(train.x.values, train.home.values, train.y.values)
print(f"train: {len(train):,} matches (1990-2014), params C={Ct:.4f} B={Bt:.4f} H={Ht:.4f}")
print(f"test : {len(test):,} matches (2015-2026), fully out-of-sample")
p_test = probs(Ct, Bt, Ht, test.x.values, test.home.values)
onehot = np.eye(3)[test.y.values]
brier_model = ((p_test - onehot) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()
base = np.array([(train.y == 0).mean(), (train.y == 1).mean(), (train.y == 2).mean()])
brier_base = ((base - onehot) ** 2).sum(axis=1).mean()
ll_model = -np.log(np.clip(p_test[np.arange(len(test)), test.y.values], 1e-12, None)).mean()
ll_base = -np.log(base[test.y.values]).mean()
print(f"3-class Brier: model {brier_model:.4f} vs base-rate baseline {brier_base:.4f} "
      f"({(1 - brier_model / brier_base) * 100:.1f}% better)")
print(f"log-loss    : model {ll_model:.4f} vs baseline {ll_base:.4f} "
      f"({(1 - ll_model / ll_base) * 100:.1f}% better)")
# Elo expectancy itself (W in {0,.5,1} vs We), same holdout
we = 1 / (10 ** (-(test.pre_home + 100 * test.home - test.pre_away) / 400) + 1)
w = np.select([test.home_score > test.away_score,
               test.home_score == test.away_score], [1.0, 0.5], 0.0)
print(f"Elo expectancy Brier (W vs We): {((we - w) ** 2).mean():.4f} vs "
      f"constant-0.5 baseline {((0.5 - w) ** 2).mean():.4f}")
# calibration: predicted home-win deciles vs observed home-win rate
dec = pd.DataFrame({"p": p_test[:, 2], "won": (test.y == 2).values})
dec["bin"] = np.clip((dec.p * 10).astype(int), 0, 9)
cal = dec.groupby("bin").agg(n=("won", "size"), pred=("p", "mean"),
                             actual=("won", "mean")).round(3)
print("calibration (predicted home-win prob decile vs observed, test set):")
print(cal.to_string())
gap = (cal.pred - cal.actual).abs().max()
print(f"max |predicted - observed| across bins: {gap:.3f}")
print("LEVEL VALIDATED: per-match outcome probabilities, out-of-sample 2015-2026.")
print("The ana_19 headline (Cape Verde's chance in ONE match vs Argentina) is a")
print("per-match probability at exactly this level; no tournament-level or")
print("multi-match aggregate is claimed or validated.")

raw_evidence.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
raw_evidence.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.

# --- ana_19: what were Cape Verde's chances against Argentina? ---
print("=== ana_19 ===")
C, B, H, nll = fit_symmetric(m.x.values, m.home.values, m.y.values)
print(f"fitted params (full sample): C={C:.4f} B={B:.4f} H={H:.4f} "
      f"(home shift = {H * 400:.0f} Elo points; mean NLL {nll:.4f})")
C_, B_, H_ = round(C, 4), round(B, 4), round(H, 4)
print(f"PUBLISHED (rounded, inlined in client_model.js): C={C_} B={B_} H={H_}, SCALE=400")
arg = elo[(elo.date == "2026-07-03") & (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde")].iloc[0]
# ratings rounded to 1 dp -- the SAME values inlined in client_model.js, so the
# browser recomputation agrees with the published numbers by construction
r_arg, r_cpv = round(arg.pre_home, 1), round(arg.pre_away, 1)
print(f"pre-match ratings 2026-07-03 (neutral venue): "
      f"Argentina {r_arg}, Cape Verde {r_cpv} (gap {r_arg - r_cpv:.1f})")
p_loss_cv, p_draw_cv, p_win_cv = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_cpv - r_arg) / 400]), 0)[0]
print(f"model, from Cape Verde's side: win in 90' {p_win_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"level after 90' (reach extra time) {p_draw_cv * 100:.1f}%, "
      f"lose in 90' {p_loss_cv * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"P(advance) if a level match is a coin flip (assumption): "
      f"{(p_win_cv + 0.5 * p_draw_cv) * 100:.1f}%")
# symmetry sanity: identical from Argentina's side
pa = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(r_arg - r_cpv) / 400]), 0)[0]
assert abs(pa[0] - p_win_cv) < 1e-12 and abs(pa[1] - p_draw_cv) < 1e-12
print("side-swap symmetry check: PASS (neutral venue, listed side irrelevant)")
# the same model across Cape Verde's whole tournament, for the record
for _, r_ in elo[(elo.tournament == "FIFA World Cup") & (elo.date >= "2026-06-01")
                 & ((elo.home_team == "Cape Verde") | (elo.away_team == "Cape Verde"))].iterrows():
    cv_home = r_.home_team == "Cape Verde"
    rcv = round(r_.pre_home if cv_home else r_.pre_away, 1)
    ropp = round(r_.pre_away if cv_home else r_.pre_home, 1)
    pl, pd_, pw = probs(C_, B_, H_, np.array([(rcv - ropp) / 400]), 0)[0]
    res = f"{int(r_.home_score)}-{int(r_.away_score)}"
    opp = r_.away_team if cv_home else r_.home_team
    print(f"  {r_.date} vs {opp} ({res}): P(CV win)={pw * 100:.1f}% "
          f"P(draw)={pd_ * 100:.1f}% P(CV loss)={pl * 100:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
raw_evidence.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.

raw_evidence.label: The Duarte family: a Schiedam mum, a Toyota Starlet, and five Rotterdam-born starters
raw_evidence.content: DutchNews interviewed Maria da Cruz of Schiedam, mother of squad brothers Laros and Deroy Duarte, on the eve of the Argentina match: 'When they're not playing I can just watch the game, but when my children play I'm chasing every ball. It's so tense.' She drove her sons to youth training across the Netherlands in a Toyota Starlet that accumulated 276,000 km. The same piece notes that FIVE Rotterdam-born players started Cape Verde's World Cup opener against Spain. After the 0-0 draw with Spain, she said, 'the boys thought: we can do this.' This is the human texture of the diaspora-squad statistic: second-generation kids raised in Dutch academies choosing the islands their parents left. Rotterdam's Cape Verdean community — which grew from sailors who settled near the port in the 1960s-70s — is the machine that produced a third of this squad's starters.

raw_evidence.label: The squad IS the diaspora: 15 of 26 born abroad, 6 in the Netherlands
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's squad_2026.csv encodes the thesis: 15 of Cape Verde's 26 World Cup players (57.7%) were born outside Cape Verde — Netherlands 6 (Jamiro Monteiro, Garry Rodrigues, Sidny Lopes Cabral, Deroy Duarte, Laros Duarte, Dailon Livramento), Portugal 4 (Jovane Cabral, Telmo Arcanjo, Wagner Pina, Helio Varela), France 3 (Logan Costa, Willy Semedo, Steven Moreira), Ireland 1 (Roberto 'Pico' Lopes, the LinkedIn call-up of det_06), United States 1 (CJ dos Santos). The squad's birth map is nearly a map of the diaspora's destinations — with one telling inversion: the Netherlands, the top birth country of the squad, does not even appear in the UN 2024 bilateral emigrant matrix (det_07). The captain and hero of the run, 39-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha, and record cap-holder Ryan Mendes were island-born, so the team is a genuine fusion, not an imported XI. Five Rotterdam-born players started the opener against Spain (det_05). For the analyst: born_abroad is a boolean column — the 15/26 split, the birth-country breakdown, and a comparison against other WC2026 squads' foreign-born shares (if computed, source squad data per country) are all chartable; do not claim Cape Verde has 'the most foreign-born squad' without computing it.

raw_evidence.label: The squad IS the diaspora: 15 of 26 born abroad, 6 in the Netherlands
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's squad_2026.csv encodes the thesis: 15 of Cape Verde's 26 World Cup players (57.7%) were born outside Cape Verde — Netherlands 6 (Jamiro Monteiro, Garry Rodrigues, Sidny Lopes Cabral, Deroy Duarte, Laros Duarte, Dailon Livramento), Portugal 4 (Jovane Cabral, Telmo Arcanjo, Wagner Pina, Helio Varela), France 3 (Logan Costa, Willy Semedo, Steven Moreira), Ireland 1 (Roberto 'Pico' Lopes, the LinkedIn call-up of det_06), United States 1 (CJ dos Santos). The squad's birth map is nearly a map of the diaspora's destinations — with one telling inversion: the Netherlands, the top birth country of the squad, does not even appear in the UN 2024 bilateral emigrant matrix (det_07). The captain and hero of the run, 39-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha, and record cap-holder Ryan Mendes were island-born, so the team is a genuine fusion, not an imported XI. Five Rotterdam-born players started the opener against Spain (det_05). For the analyst: born_abroad is a boolean column — the 15/26 split, the birth-country breakdown, and a comparison against other WC2026 squads' foreign-born shares (if computed, source squad data per country) are all chartable; do not claim Cape Verde has 'the most foreign-born squad' without computing it.

for c, v in bc.items():
    print(f"  {c}: {v}")
pos_split = s.groupby("pos").born_abroad.agg(["sum", "count"])
print("by position (born_abroad / total):")
for p_, row in pos_split.iterrows():
    print(f"  {p_}: {int(row['sum'])}/{int(row['count'])}")

print(f"youngest: {yng['name']} {yng.age_20260703:.1f}y (b. {yng.dob}, {yng.birth_country})")

The imported share is highest in midfield (8 of 12) and defence (5 of 8). The generational sweep runs from island-born captain Vozinha, who turned 40 during the group stage (b. 1986-06-03 -- match reports calling him 39 are wrong by a month), to Portugal-born Wagner Pina (23.7).

abroad = s[s.born_abroad]

for c, v in bc.items():
    print(f"  {c}: {v}")
pos_split = s.groupby("pos").born_abroad.agg(["sum", "count"])
print("by position (born_abroad / total):")
for p_, row in pos_split.iterrows():
    print(f"  {p_}: {int(row['sum'])}/{int(row['count'])}")

old = s.loc[s.age_20260703.idxmax()]
yng = s.loc[s.age_20260703.idxmin()]
print(f"oldest : {old['name']} {old.age_20260703:.1f}y (b. {old.dob}, {old.birth_country})")
print(f"youngest: {yng['name']} {yng.age_20260703:.1f}y (b. {yng.dob}, {yng.birth_country})")

raw_evidence.label: Half the caps, 3 of 4 World Cup goals came from abroad-born players
raw_evidence.content: The 15 abroad-born players carry 414 of the squad's 823 career caps (50.3%) and 33 of its 75 pre-tournament goals (44.0%) -- so the diaspora contingent is not padding, it is half the team's entire international experience. At the World Cup itself the tilt was stronger: of Cape Verde's four tournament goals, three were scored by players born abroad -- Helio Varela (b. Portugal) vs Uruguay, and both goals against Argentina by Rotterdam-born Deroy Duarte and Sidny Lopes Cabral (det_04); only Kevin Pina's vs Uruguay came from an island-born player. The data also confirms det_04's detail: Duarte entered the tournament with 0 international goals in 33 caps -- his 59th-minute equaliser against the world champions was his first. Counterweight: the record-holder is island-born Ryan Mendes (96 caps, 22 goals).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_10: caps & goals by birth group; WC2026 goals traced ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")
grp = s.groupby("born_abroad")[["caps", "goals"]].sum()
tot_caps, tot_goals = s.caps.sum(), s.goals.sum()
ab_caps, ab_goals = grp.loc[True, "caps"], grp.loc[True, "goals"]
print(f"total caps: {tot_caps}, from born-abroad players: {ab_caps} "
      f"({ab_caps / tot_caps * 100:.1f}%)")
print(f"total pre-tournament goals: {tot_goals}, from born-abroad players: {ab_goals} "
      f"({ab_goals / tot_goals * 100:.1f}%)")
top_scorer = s.loc[s.goals.idxmax()]
print(f"top pre-tournament scorer: {top_scorer['name']} ({int(top_scorer.goals)} goals, "
      f"{int(top_scorer.caps)} caps, born {top_scorer.birth_country})")
by_country = s.groupby("birth_country")[["caps", "goals"]].sum().join(
    s.birth_country.value_counts().rename("players")).sort_values("players", ascending=False)
print(by_country.to_string())
# WC2026 goals: scorers per det_01 (vs Argentina) and det_02 (vs Uruguay)
wc_scorers = ["Kevin Pina", "Hélio Varela", "Deroy Duarte", "Sidny Lopes Cabral"]
print("WC2026 goalscorers traced to birth country (det_01/det_02 + squad csv):")
for nm in wc_scorers:
    row = s[s.name == nm].iloc[0]
    print(f"  {nm}: born {row.birth_country} (caps {int(row.caps)}, "
          f"pre-tournament goals {int(row.goals)})")
n_abroad_goals = sum(s[s.name == nm].iloc[0].born_abroad for nm in wc_scorers)
print(f"WC2026 goals by born-abroad players: {n_abroad_goals}/4; "
      f"both Argentina-match scorers born in the Netherlands (Rotterdam, det_04)")
print("cross-check det_04: Deroy Duarte pre-tournament goals = "
      f"{int(s[s.name == 'Deroy Duarte'].iloc[0].goals)} "
      "(his 59' vs Argentina was indeed his first international goal)")

raw_evidence.label: The squad IS the diaspora: 15 of 26 born abroad, 6 in the Netherlands
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's squad_2026.csv encodes the thesis: 15 of Cape Verde's 26 World Cup players (57.7%) were born outside Cape Verde — Netherlands 6 (Jamiro Monteiro, Garry Rodrigues, Sidny Lopes Cabral, Deroy Duarte, Laros Duarte, Dailon Livramento), Portugal 4 (Jovane Cabral, Telmo Arcanjo, Wagner Pina, Helio Varela), France 3 (Logan Costa, Willy Semedo, Steven Moreira), Ireland 1 (Roberto 'Pico' Lopes, the LinkedIn call-up of det_06), United States 1 (CJ dos Santos). The squad's birth map is nearly a map of the diaspora's destinations — with one telling inversion: the Netherlands, the top birth country of the squad, does not even appear in the UN 2024 bilateral emigrant matrix (det_07). The captain and hero of the run, 39-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha, and record cap-holder Ryan Mendes were island-born, so the team is a genuine fusion, not an imported XI. Five Rotterdam-born players started the opener against Spain (det_05). For the analyst: born_abroad is a boolean column — the 15/26 split, the birth-country breakdown, and a comparison against other WC2026 squads' foreign-born shares (if computed, source squad data per country) are all chartable; do not claim Cape Verde has 'the most foreign-born squad' without computing it.

raw_evidence.label: Bubista and the FCF's deliberate diaspora-recruitment machine
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde's rise is not an accident of eligibility rules — it is a two-decade federation strategy executed by a home-grown coach. Pedro Leitao Brito, 'Bubista' (b. 6 January 1970, Boa Vista, Cape Verde; 21 caps as a centre-back 1989-2005), was appointed head coach in January 2020, qualified the team for consecutive AFCONs (2021, 2023), delivered the historic 2026 World Cup qualification, and was named CAF Coach of the Year 2025. Since 2002 the federation has systematically recruited players developed abroad — in Portugal, France, the Netherlands and Ireland — among the children of emigrants. The emblematic story: in 2019, then-coach Rui Aguas contacted Shamrock Rovers defender Roberto Lopes ('Pico', squad no. 4, born in Dublin to a Cape Verdean father) via LINKEDIN to persuade him to play for Cape Verde. Under FIFA rules a player must hold the nationality and not have played a competitive senior match for another country — so Cape Verde's scouts work Europe's youth academies, pitching dual-nationals on representing their parents' islands. Bubista's man-management task is then to fuse Portugal-based, Netherlands-based and island-based players into one dressing room.

raw_evidence.label: Not one of the 26 plays club football in Cape Verde
raw_evidence.content: The squad's club map is as diasporic as its birth map: the 26 players are employed in 14 different countries, and exactly zero play in Cape Verde's domestic league. Portugal hosts the most (7), then Turkey (3), with Bulgaria, the US, Cyprus and Russia at 2 each, and single players in Romania, Spain, Ireland, the UAE, Hungary, the Netherlands, Finland and Israel. Cape Verde's entire World Cup team is an export product -- even its island-born players professionalised abroad.

      f"{int((s.club_country == 'CPV').sum())}")
for c, v in cc.items():
    print(f"  {c}: {v}")

Source: UN DESA International Migrant Stock 2024 (POP/DB/MIG/Stock/Rev.2024) (https://www.un.org/development/desa/pd/content/international-migrant-stock) Facts: World total of international migrants born in Cabo Verde: 146,396 at mid-2024; The 2024 destination-by-origin matrix lists only 24 named destinations for origin Cabo Verde; Netherlands, United States, Spain and Senegal have no row Source: EUDiF Diaspora Engagement Mapping: Cabo Verde (AFFORD/EUDiF, updated December 2023) (https://diasporafordevelopment.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/CF_Cabo-Verde-v.1.p) Facts: Emigrants = 186,372, about 31% of the total population (from UNDESA Migration Stock Statistics 2019); Top destinations (UNDESA 2019): Portugal 60,543; United States 43,729; France 24,545; Netherlands 12,601; Angola 9,400; Senegal is another significant destination

raw_evidence.label: The UN count is a floor: 146,396 born-in-CV emigrants, with the biggest hosts missing
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's UN DESA 2024 bilateral matrix records 146,396 people born in Cabo Verde living abroad (world total, mid-2024) across only 24 named destinations — and the Netherlands, United States, Spain and Senegal are entirely absent as destination rows, because those countries' statistics do not break out small origin groups in the 2024 revision. The absence is structural, not real: the PREVIOUS UN revision (UNDESA 2019 migrant stock, as tabulated in the EUDiF diaspora factsheet) counted Portugal 60,543, United States 43,729, France 24,545, Netherlands 12,601 and Angola 9,400 as the top destinations for Cabo Verde-born migrants, with 186,372 emigrants in total (~31% of the resident population). So the 2024 matrix's 146k world total is a hard floor on the born-in-Cape-Verde diaspora, and any chart built from the bilateral file must say so. Rule for every downstream role: never present the UN bilateral numbers as 'the diaspora' — they are the first, strictest of three layers (born-in-CV migrants < citizens abroad < heritage/ancestry diaspora).

raw_evidence.content: The dataset's UN DESA 2024 bilateral matrix records 146,396 people born in Cabo Verde living abroad (world total, mid-2024) across only 24 named destinations — and the Netherlands, United States, Spain and Senegal are entirely absent as destination rows, because those countries' statistics do not break out small origin groups in the 2024 revision. Rule for every downstream role: never present the UN bilateral numbers as 'the diaspora' — they are the first, strictest of three layers (born-in-CV migrants < citizens abroad < heritage/ancestry diaspora).

raw_evidence.label: The UN count is a floor: 146,396 born-in-CV emigrants, with the biggest hosts missing
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's UN DESA 2024 bilateral matrix records 146,396 people born in Cabo Verde living abroad (world total, mid-2024) across only 24 named destinations — and the Netherlands, United States, Spain and Senegal are entirely absent as destination rows, because those countries' statistics do not break out small origin groups in the 2024 revision. The absence is structural, not real: the PREVIOUS UN revision (UNDESA 2019 migrant stock, as tabulated in the EUDiF diaspora factsheet) counted Portugal 60,543, United States 43,729, France 24,545, Netherlands 12,601 and Angola 9,400 as the top destinations for Cabo Verde-born migrants, with 186,372 emigrants in total (~31% of the resident population). So the 2024 matrix's 146k world total is a hard floor on the born-in-Cape-Verde diaspora, and any chart built from the bilateral file must say so. Rule for every downstream role: never present the UN bilateral numbers as 'the diaspora' — they are the first, strictest of three layers (born-in-CV migrants < citizens abroad < heritage/ancestry diaspora).

raw_evidence.label: The UN floor alone equals 28% of the resident population
raw_evidence.content: Even on the strictest possible definition -- born in Cabo Verde, alive, abroad, counted by a destination that reports small origins -- the diaspora has doubled relative to the home population in one generation: from 13.8% of residents in 1990 to 27.9% in 2024 (146,396 counted emigrants vs 524,877 residents). Every heritage-layer estimate (det_07/det_08: ~700k-1M+ including descendants) sits far above this line; the chart of this series should be labelled as the floor it is.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_04: UN emigrant floor vs resident population, 1990-2024 ---
print("=== ana_04 ===")

    ratio = world[y] / cpv_pop[y] * 100
    rows04.append((y, int(world[y]), int(cpv_pop[y]), round(ratio, 1)))
    print(f"  {y} | {int(world[y]):>7,} | {int(cpv_pop[y]):>7,} | {ratio:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: The UN floor alone equals 28% of the resident population
raw_evidence.content: Even on the strictest possible definition -- born in Cabo Verde, alive, abroad, counted by a destination that reports small origins -- the diaspora has doubled relative to the home population in one generation: from 13.8% of residents in 1990 to 27.9% in 2024 (146,396 counted emigrants vs 524,877 residents). Every heritage-layer estimate (det_07/det_08: ~700k-1M+ including descendants) sits far above this line; the chart of this series should be labelled as the floor it is.

raw_evidence.label: Top-20 worldwide in emigrants-per-resident, on the floor count
raw_evidence.content: Reading per-origin world totals from the full UN 2024 matrix and dividing by World Bank 2024 populations, Cabo Verde's counted-emigrant floor (146,396 = 27.9% of residents) ranks #20 of 212 WB-covered origins worldwide, and #2 in Sub-Saharan Africa behind only Comoros (42.4%) -- ahead of South Sudan (26.5%) and Eritrea (25.8%), whose emigration is war-driven. Nearly everything above Cabo Verde is a war economy (West Bank and Gaza 80.0%, Syria 36.2%, Venezuela 29.3%), a Balkan or Caribbean emigration state (Albania 51.2%, Bosnia 50.8%, Jamaica 44.0%, Guyana 56.5%), or a microstate (Monaco 95.0%, Samoa 54.7%, Tonga 51.1%). And Cabo Verde's true position is HIGHER: its four biggest missing host countries (Netherlands, US, Spain, Senegal) are exactly the ones its floor count omits.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_05: Global rank of emigrant floor as % of resident population ---
print("=== ana_05 ===")
# Per-origin world totals from the raw UN DESA matrix (dest_code 900 = World).
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(P("01_diaspora", "undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx"),
                            read_only=True)
ws = wb["Table 1"]
origin_tot = {}
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=12, max_col=15, values_only=True):
    (_i, dst, _cov, _dt, dcode, origin, ocode, *vals) = row
    if dcode is None or origin is None or ocode is None:
        continue
    if int(dcode) == 900 and int(ocode) < 900:  # World row, individual origin
        v = vals[7]  # 2024 wave
        if v not in (None, "", ".."):
            origin_tot[origin.replace("*", "").strip()] = int(v)
print(f"origins with a 2024 world-total row: {len(origin_tot)}")

meta = pd.read_csv(P("04_population",
                     "Metadata_Country_API_SP.POP.TOTL_DS2_EN_csv_v2_3107.csv"),
                   encoding="utf-8-sig")
countries = meta[meta.Region.notna()]  # drop WB aggregates (World, regions, ...)
pop24 = pop[pop.year == 2024].merge(countries[["Country Code"]], on="Country Code")
pop_by_name = pop24.set_index("Country Name").population

UN_TO_WB = {  # UN DESA location name -> WB WDI Country Name (only mismatches)
    "United States of America": "United States", "Republic of Korea": "Korea, Rep.",

    "Iran (Islamic Republic of)": "Iran, Islamic Rep.",

    "Bolivia (Plurinational State of)": "Bolivia", "Egypt": "Egypt, Arab Rep.",
    "Yemen": "Yemen, Rep.", "Gambia": "Gambia, The", "Bahamas": "Bahamas, The",
    "Democratic Republic of the Congo": "Congo, Dem. Rep.", "Congo": "Congo, Rep.",
    "Micronesia (Fed. States of)": "Micronesia, Fed. Sts.",
    "Saint Lucia": "St. Lucia", "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines": "St. Vincent and the Grenadines",
    "Saint Kitts and Nevis": "St. Kitts and Nevis", "Saint Martin (French part)": "St. Martin (French part)",
    "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)": "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)",
    "Kyrgyzstan": "Kyrgyz Republic", "Slovakia": "Slovak Republic",
    "Lao People's Democratic Republic": "Lao PDR",
    "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong SAR, China", "China, Macao SAR": "Macao SAR, China",
    "State of Palestine": "West Bank and Gaza", "Cote d'Ivoire": "Cote d'Ivoire",
    "Turkiye": "Turkiye", "Viet Nam": "Viet Nam",
    "United Republic of Tanzania": "Tanzania", "Republic of Moldova": "Moldova",
    "Brunei Darussalam": "Brunei Darussalam", "Curacao": "Curacao",
    "Syrian Arab Republic": "Syrian Arab Republic",
}
def to_wb(name):
    # normalize accents the two sources spell differently
    n = (name.replace("ô", "o").replace("ç", "c").replace("ü", "u")
             .replace("é", "e").replace("è", "e"))
    return UN_TO_WB.get(name, UN_TO_WB.get(n, name))

rows05, unmatched = [], []
for origin, emig in origin_tot.items():
    wb_name = to_wb(origin)
    if wb_name in pop_by_name.index:
        p24 = pop_by_name[wb_name]
        rows05.append((wb_name, emig, int(p24), round(emig / p24 * 100, 1)))
    else:
        unmatched.append((origin, emig))

                                   "ratio_pct"]).sort_values("ratio_pct", ascending=False)
rk["rank"] = range(1, len(rk) + 1)

print("largest excluded origins:", sorted(unmatched, key=lambda x: -x[1])[:8])
print(rk.head(25).to_string(index=False))
cv_row = rk[rk.origin == "Cabo Verde"].iloc[0]
print(f"Cabo Verde: rank #{int(cv_row['rank'])} of {len(rk)} "
      f"(emigrant floor {cv_row.emigrants_2024:,} = {cv_row.ratio_pct}% of residents)")
africa = countries[countries.Region == "Sub-Saharan Africa"]["Country Code"]
af_names = set(pop24[pop24["Country Code"].isin(africa)]["Country Name"])
rk_af = rk[rk.origin.isin(af_names)].reset_index(drop=True)
print("Sub-Saharan Africa top 5 by ratio:")
print(rk_af.head(5).to_string(index=False))

Source: Cape Verdeans in the Netherlands — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verdeans_in_the_Netherlands) Facts: CBS: approximately 23,150 people of Cape Verdean migration background in the Netherlands (2022); About 90% live in the Rotterdam metropolitan area; largest concentration in Delfshaven (~8.8% of the borough)

raw_evidence.label: The heritage layer, Netherlands: ~23,000 by CBS count, 90% around Rotterdam
raw_evidence.content: The Netherlands is the squad's biggest birthplace (6 of the 26 players) and hosts one of the most concentrated Cape Verdean communities anywhere. Statistics Netherlands (CBS) counted roughly 23,150 people of Cape Verdean migration background in 2022 — versus just 12,601 born-in-Cape-Verde migrants in the UN's 2019 stock, another clean demonstration of the migrant-stock vs heritage gap. About 90% live in the Rotterdam metropolitan area; in the borough of Delfshaven they are about 8.8% of the population, and community estimates for Rotterdam run to 20,000-30,000 — often described as the largest Cape Verdean community in any city outside the islands. The community's origin is maritime: young Cape Verdean men signed on as sailors on Dutch ships in the 1960s-70s and settled by the port. Half a century later, that settlement pattern is producing World Cup goal scorers.

Source: Cape Verdean Americans — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verdean_Americans) Facts: ACS 2023: 106,084 Americans with Cape Verdean ancestry; 2024 estimate 142,570; Massachusetts (~90,118) and Rhode Island (~26,376) host the vast majority Source: Building on 200 Years of Historic United States-Cabo Verde Ties — U.S. Department of State (https://2017-2021.state.gov/building-on-200-years-of-historic-united-states-cabo) Facts: The State Department describes approximately half a million Americans of Cape Verdean descent, mainly in New England

raw_evidence.label: The heritage layer, USA: ~106-143k self-reported vs 'half a million' of Cape Verdean descent
raw_evidence.content: The United States hosts the largest Cape Verdean community in the world — but its size depends entirely on the definition, and the story brief's shorthand ('US ACS Cape Verdean ancestry ~500k') conflates two different numbers that must not be blurred. The self-reported census figure: the American Community Survey counted 106,084 Americans reporting Cape Verdean ancestry (2023), rising to 142,570 in the 2024 estimates, concentrated overwhelmingly in Massachusetts (~90,118) and Rhode Island (~26,376), with Brockton MA (16,753), Boston (13,605), New Bedford (9,613) and Pawtucket RI (8,092) the biggest city communities. The descent estimate: the U.S. State Department's own account of 200 years of US-Cabo Verde ties puts 'approximately 500,000' Americans of Cape Verdean descent in New England — a number echoed by community organizations — and a 2007 New York Times report estimated 265,000 Cape Verdean immigrants and descendants. The gap between 106k (self-identified, ACS) and 500k (descent, State Dept) is itself a story: generations of Cape Verdeans arrived before the country existed (pre-1975 they traveled on Portuguese documents) and were folded into Portuguese-American or Black American identities. Use ACS numbers for charts; use the 500k only as an attributed descent estimate in prose.

sentences.context: Cape Verde's own state is built around this arithmetic.
sentences.summary: det_11: A state built for its emigrants: 6 diaspora MPs, external voting, dual citizenship. Source: EUDiF Diaspora Engagement Mapping: Cabo Verde (AFFORD/EUDiF, updated December 2023) (https://diasporafordevelopment.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/CF_Cabo-Verde-v.1.p) Facts: Cape Verdeans abroad have voted in presidential and legislative elections since 1992; Six members of parliament represent citizens abroad: two each from the Americas, the rest of Africa, and Europe

raw_evidence.label: A state built for its emigrants: 6 diaspora MPs, external voting, dual citizenship
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde is one of the few countries whose constitution and parliament are explicitly architected around the fact that most of its people live abroad. Cape Verdeans abroad have voted in presidential and legislative elections since 1992; six seats in the National Assembly are reserved for the diaspora (two each for the Americas, Africa and Europe); a vote-weighting system was implemented precisely 'to avoid compromising national independence as more Cape Verdeans live abroad than in the national territory'; and Article 40 of the constitution guarantees that no one Cape Verdean by origin may be deprived of nationality — dual citizenship is a birthright, which is also what makes the football federation's diaspora recruitment legally frictionless. The EUDiF diaspora-engagement mapping puts the total diaspora at close to 120% of the resident population, and successive governments have run dedicated diaspora institutions (Institute of Communities 2001, Ministry of Communities 2011, folded into Foreign Affairs 2016), an Emigrant Investor Statute (2020) with special tax incentives, and 'ethnic tourism' promotion aimed at the diaspora itself.

raw_evidence.label: A state built for its emigrants: 6 diaspora MPs, external voting, dual citizenship
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde is one of the few countries whose constitution and parliament are explicitly architected around the fact that most of its people live abroad. Cape Verdeans abroad have voted in presidential and legislative elections since 1992; six seats in the National Assembly are reserved for the diaspora (two each for the Americas, Africa and Europe); a vote-weighting system was implemented precisely 'to avoid compromising national independence as more Cape Verdeans live abroad than in the national territory'; and Article 40 of the constitution guarantees that no one Cape Verdean by origin may be deprived of nationality — dual citizenship is a birthright, which is also what makes the football federation's diaspora recruitment legally frictionless. The EUDiF diaspora-engagement mapping puts the total diaspora at close to 120% of the resident population, and successive governments have run dedicated diaspora institutions (Institute of Communities 2001, Ministry of Communities 2011, folded into Foreign Affairs 2016), an Emigrant Investor Statute (2020) with special tax incentives, and 'ethnic tourism' promotion aimed at the diaspora itself.

raw_evidence.label: Top-20 worldwide in emigrants-per-resident, on the floor count
raw_evidence.content: Reading per-origin world totals from the full UN 2024 matrix and dividing by World Bank 2024 populations, Cabo Verde's counted-emigrant floor (146,396 = 27.9% of residents) ranks #20 of 212 WB-covered origins worldwide, and #2 in Sub-Saharan Africa behind only Comoros (42.4%) -- ahead of South Sudan (26.5%) and Eritrea (25.8%), whose emigration is war-driven. Nearly everything above Cabo Verde is a war economy (West Bank and Gaza 80.0%, Syria 36.2%, Venezuela 29.3%), a Balkan or Caribbean emigration state (Albania 51.2%, Bosnia 50.8%, Jamaica 44.0%, Guyana 56.5%), or a microstate (Monaco 95.0%, Samoa 54.7%, Tonga 51.1%). And Cabo Verde's true position is HIGHER: its four biggest missing host countries (Netherlands, US, Spain, Senegal) are exactly the ones its floor count omits.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_05: Global rank of emigrant floor as % of resident population ---
print("=== ana_05 ===")
# Per-origin world totals from the raw UN DESA matrix (dest_code 900 = World).
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(P("01_diaspora", "undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx"),
                            read_only=True)
ws = wb["Table 1"]
origin_tot = {}
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=12, max_col=15, values_only=True):
    (_i, dst, _cov, _dt, dcode, origin, ocode, *vals) = row
    if dcode is None or origin is None or ocode is None:
        continue
    if int(dcode) == 900 and int(ocode) < 900:  # World row, individual origin
        v = vals[7]  # 2024 wave
        if v not in (None, "", ".."):
            origin_tot[origin.replace("*", "").strip()] = int(v)
print(f"origins with a 2024 world-total row: {len(origin_tot)}")

meta = pd.read_csv(P("04_population",
                     "Metadata_Country_API_SP.POP.TOTL_DS2_EN_csv_v2_3107.csv"),
                   encoding="utf-8-sig")
countries = meta[meta.Region.notna()]  # drop WB aggregates (World, regions, ...)
pop24 = pop[pop.year == 2024].merge(countries[["Country Code"]], on="Country Code")
pop_by_name = pop24.set_index("Country Name").population

UN_TO_WB = {  # UN DESA location name -> WB WDI Country Name (only mismatches)
    "United States of America": "United States", "Republic of Korea": "Korea, Rep.",
    "Dem. People's Republic of Korea": "Korea, Dem. People's Rep.",
    "Iran (Islamic Republic of)": "Iran, Islamic Rep.",
    "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)": "Venezuela, RB",
    "Bolivia (Plurinational State of)": "Bolivia", "Egypt": "Egypt, Arab Rep.",
    "Yemen": "Yemen, Rep.", "Gambia": "Gambia, The", "Bahamas": "Bahamas, The",
    "Democratic Republic of the Congo": "Congo, Dem. Rep.", "Congo": "Congo, Rep.",
    "Micronesia (Fed. States of)": "Micronesia, Fed. Sts.",
    "Saint Lucia": "St. Lucia", "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines": "St. Vincent and the Grenadines",
    "Saint Kitts and Nevis": "St. Kitts and Nevis", "Saint Martin (French part)": "St. Martin (French part)",
    "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)": "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)",
    "Kyrgyzstan": "Kyrgyz Republic", "Slovakia": "Slovak Republic",
    "Lao People's Democratic Republic": "Lao PDR",
    "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong SAR, China", "China, Macao SAR": "Macao SAR, China",
    "State of Palestine": "West Bank and Gaza", "Cote d'Ivoire": "Cote d'Ivoire",
    "Turkiye": "Turkiye", "Viet Nam": "Viet Nam",
    "United Republic of Tanzania": "Tanzania", "Republic of Moldova": "Moldova",
    "Brunei Darussalam": "Brunei Darussalam", "Curacao": "Curacao",
    "Syrian Arab Republic": "Syrian Arab Republic",
}
def to_wb(name):
    # normalize accents the two sources spell differently
    n = (name.replace("ô", "o").replace("ç", "c").replace("ü", "u")
             .replace("é", "e").replace("è", "e"))
    return UN_TO_WB.get(name, UN_TO_WB.get(n, name))

rows05, unmatched = [], []
for origin, emig in origin_tot.items():
    wb_name = to_wb(origin)
    if wb_name in pop_by_name.index:
        p24 = pop_by_name[wb_name]
        rows05.append((wb_name, emig, int(p24), round(emig / p24 * 100, 1)))
    else:
        unmatched.append((origin, emig))
rk = pd.DataFrame(rows05, columns=["origin", "emigrants_2024", "population_2024",
                                   "ratio_pct"]).sort_values("ratio_pct", ascending=False)
rk["rank"] = range(1, len(rk) + 1)
print(f"matched origins: {len(rk)}; unmatched (no WB population row, excluded): {len(unmatched)}")
print("largest excluded origins:", sorted(unmatched, key=lambda x: -x[1])[:8])
print(rk.head(25).to_string(index=False))
cv_row = rk[rk.origin == "Cabo Verde"].iloc[0]
print(f"Cabo Verde: rank #{int(cv_row['rank'])} of {len(rk)} "
      f"(emigrant floor {cv_row.emigrants_2024:,} = {cv_row.ratio_pct}% of residents)")
africa = countries[countries.Region == "Sub-Saharan Africa"]["Country Code"]
af_names = set(pop24[pop24["Country Code"].isin(africa)]["Country Name"])
rk_af = rk[rk.origin.isin(af_names)].reset_index(drop=True)
print("Sub-Saharan Africa top 5 by ratio:")
print(rk_af.head(5).to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_05: Global rank of emigrant floor as % of resident population ---
print("=== ana_05 ===")
# Per-origin world totals from the raw UN DESA matrix (dest_code 900 = World).
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(P("01_diaspora", "undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx"),
                            read_only=True)
ws = wb["Table 1"]
origin_tot = {}
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=12, max_col=15, values_only=True):
    (_i, dst, _cov, _dt, dcode, origin, ocode, *vals) = row
    if dcode is None or origin is None or ocode is None:

    if int(dcode) == 900 and int(ocode) < 900:  # World row, individual origin

    "Lao People's Democratic Republic": "Lao PDR",
    "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong SAR, China", "China, Macao SAR": "Macao SAR, China",

raw_evidence.label: Top-20 worldwide in emigrants-per-resident, on the floor count
raw_evidence.content: Reading per-origin world totals from the full UN 2024 matrix and dividing by World Bank 2024 populations, Cabo Verde's counted-emigrant floor (146,396 = 27.9% of residents) ranks #20 of 212 WB-covered origins worldwide, and #2 in Sub-Saharan Africa behind only Comoros (42.4%) -- ahead of South Sudan (26.5%) and Eritrea (25.8%), whose emigration is war-driven. Nearly everything above Cabo Verde is a war economy (West Bank and Gaza 80.0%, Syria 36.2%, Venezuela 29.3%), a Balkan or Caribbean emigration state (Albania 51.2%, Bosnia 50.8%, Jamaica 44.0%, Guyana 56.5%), or a microstate (Monaco 95.0%, Samoa 54.7%, Tonga 51.1%). And Cabo Verde's true position is HIGHER: its four biggest missing host countries (Netherlands, US, Spain, Senegal) are exactly the ones its floor count omits.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_05: Global rank of emigrant floor as % of resident population ---
print("=== ana_05 ===")
# Per-origin world totals from the raw UN DESA matrix (dest_code 900 = World).
wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(P("01_diaspora", "undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx"),
                            read_only=True)
ws = wb["Table 1"]
origin_tot = {}
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=12, max_col=15, values_only=True):
    (_i, dst, _cov, _dt, dcode, origin, ocode, *vals) = row
    if dcode is None or origin is None or ocode is None:
        continue
    if int(dcode) == 900 and int(ocode) < 900:  # World row, individual origin
        v = vals[7]  # 2024 wave
        if v not in (None, "", ".."):
            origin_tot[origin.replace("*", "").strip()] = int(v)
print(f"origins with a 2024 world-total row: {len(origin_tot)}")

meta = pd.read_csv(P("04_population",
                     "Metadata_Country_API_SP.POP.TOTL_DS2_EN_csv_v2_3107.csv"),
                   encoding="utf-8-sig")
countries = meta[meta.Region.notna()]  # drop WB aggregates (World, regions, ...)
pop24 = pop[pop.year == 2024].merge(countries[["Country Code"]], on="Country Code")
pop_by_name = pop24.set_index("Country Name").population

UN_TO_WB = {  # UN DESA location name -> WB WDI Country Name (only mismatches)
    "United States of America": "United States", "Republic of Korea": "Korea, Rep.",
    "Dem. People's Republic of Korea": "Korea, Dem. People's Rep.",
    "Iran (Islamic Republic of)": "Iran, Islamic Rep.",
    "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)": "Venezuela, RB",
    "Bolivia (Plurinational State of)": "Bolivia", "Egypt": "Egypt, Arab Rep.",
    "Yemen": "Yemen, Rep.", "Gambia": "Gambia, The", "Bahamas": "Bahamas, The",
    "Democratic Republic of the Congo": "Congo, Dem. Rep.", "Congo": "Congo, Rep.",
    "Micronesia (Fed. States of)": "Micronesia, Fed. Sts.",
    "Saint Lucia": "St. Lucia", "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines": "St. Vincent and the Grenadines",
    "Saint Kitts and Nevis": "St. Kitts and Nevis", "Saint Martin (French part)": "St. Martin (French part)",
    "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)": "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)",
    "Kyrgyzstan": "Kyrgyz Republic", "Slovakia": "Slovak Republic",
    "Lao People's Democratic Republic": "Lao PDR",
    "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong SAR, China", "China, Macao SAR": "Macao SAR, China",
    "State of Palestine": "West Bank and Gaza", "Cote d'Ivoire": "Cote d'Ivoire",
    "Turkiye": "Turkiye", "Viet Nam": "Viet Nam",
    "United Republic of Tanzania": "Tanzania", "Republic of Moldova": "Moldova",
    "Brunei Darussalam": "Brunei Darussalam", "Curacao": "Curacao",
    "Syrian Arab Republic": "Syrian Arab Republic",
}
def to_wb(name):
    # normalize accents the two sources spell differently
    n = (name.replace("ô", "o").replace("ç", "c").replace("ü", "u")
             .replace("é", "e").replace("è", "e"))
    return UN_TO_WB.get(name, UN_TO_WB.get(n, name))

rows05, unmatched = [], []
for origin, emig in origin_tot.items():
    wb_name = to_wb(origin)
    if wb_name in pop_by_name.index:
        p24 = pop_by_name[wb_name]
        rows05.append((wb_name, emig, int(p24), round(emig / p24 * 100, 1)))
    else:
        unmatched.append((origin, emig))
rk = pd.DataFrame(rows05, columns=["origin", "emigrants_2024", "population_2024",
                                   "ratio_pct"]).sort_values("ratio_pct", ascending=False)
rk["rank"] = range(1, len(rk) + 1)
print(f"matched origins: {len(rk)}; unmatched (no WB population row, excluded): {len(unmatched)}")
print("largest excluded origins:", sorted(unmatched, key=lambda x: -x[1])[:8])
print(rk.head(25).to_string(index=False))
cv_row = rk[rk.origin == "Cabo Verde"].iloc[0]
print(f"Cabo Verde: rank #{int(cv_row['rank'])} of {len(rk)} "
      f"(emigrant floor {cv_row.emigrants_2024:,} = {cv_row.ratio_pct}% of residents)")
africa = countries[countries.Region == "Sub-Saharan Africa"]["Country Code"]
af_names = set(pop24[pop24["Country Code"].isin(africa)]["Country Name"])
rk_af = rk[rk.origin.isin(af_names)].reset_index(drop=True)
print("Sub-Saharan Africa top 5 by ratio:")
print(rk_af.head(5).to_string(index=False))

 Comoros 42.4 (#9) | Cabo Verde 27.9 (#20) | South Sudan 26.5 (#22) | Eritrea 25.8 (#24) | Seychelles 18.3 (#35)

wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(P("01_diaspora", "undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx"),

origin_tot = {}
for row in ws.iter_rows(min_row=12, max_col=15, values_only=True):

    "Micronesia (Fed. States of)": "Micronesia, Fed. Sts.",
    "Saint Lucia": "St. Lucia", "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines": "St. Vincent and the Grenadines",
    "Saint Kitts and Nevis": "St. Kitts and Nevis", "Saint Martin (French part)": "St. Martin (French part)",
    "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)": "Sint Maarten (Dutch part)",
    "Kyrgyzstan": "Kyrgyz Republic", "Slovakia": "Slovak Republic",
    "Lao People's Democratic Republic": "Lao PDR",
    "China, Hong Kong SAR": "Hong Kong SAR, China", "China, Macao SAR": "Macao SAR, China",
    "State of Palestine": "West Bank and Gaza", "Cote d'Ivoire": "Cote d'Ivoire",
    "Turkiye": "Turkiye", "Viet Nam": "Viet Nam",

             .replace("é", "e").replace("è", "e"))

raw_evidence.label: Why the diaspora is structural: famine, whaling ships, and colonial neglect
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verdean emigration is not a modern labour-market choice — it began as survival. The Sahelian archipelago, colonized by Portugal from the 1460s and a hub of the Atlantic slave trade, suffered repeated catastrophic famines: Wikipedia's tally records 11 major famines between 1580 and 1866 (including ~30,000 deaths in 1830-33 and 20,000-30,000 in 1863-66), and the two worst of the 20th century — 1941-43 and 1947-48, under Salazar's Estado Novo — killed an estimated 45,000 people while the colonial government failed to supply food aid or improve water access. On individual islands the toll reached 28% (Sao Nicolau) and 31% (Fogo) of the population. Between 1900 and 1970 about 80,000 Cape Verdeans were shipped as contract labourers to the cocoa plantations of Portuguese Sao Tome and Principe — which is why Sao Tome appears in the UN emigrant-stock data with a shrinking, ageing community (4,250 in 1990 down to 1,115 in 2024). The escape route west was older still: from the early 1800s, New England whaling ships recruited crews in the islands, and by the mid-1800s New Bedford, Massachusetts became the anchor of Cape Verdean America, later supplemented by cranberry-bog labour in southeastern Massachusetts. Emigration accelerated after 1869 amid drought, starvation and economic decline; US restrictionist laws in 1922 choked it off; the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act reopened it. Independence arrived only in 1975, after the joint liberation struggle with Guinea-Bissau. The result: a nation whose defining infrastructure is the emigrant network itself.

raw_evidence.label: Why the diaspora is structural: famine, whaling ships, and colonial neglect
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verdean emigration is not a modern labour-market choice — it began as survival. The Sahelian archipelago, colonized by Portugal from the 1460s and a hub of the Atlantic slave trade, suffered repeated catastrophic famines: Wikipedia's tally records 11 major famines between 1580 and 1866 (including ~30,000 deaths in 1830-33 and 20,000-30,000 in 1863-66), and the two worst of the 20th century — 1941-43 and 1947-48, under Salazar's Estado Novo — killed an estimated 45,000 people while the colonial government failed to supply food aid or improve water access. On individual islands the toll reached 28% (Sao Nicolau) and 31% (Fogo) of the population. Between 1900 and 1970 about 80,000 Cape Verdeans were shipped as contract labourers to the cocoa plantations of Portuguese Sao Tome and Principe — which is why Sao Tome appears in the UN emigrant-stock data with a shrinking, ageing community (4,250 in 1990 down to 1,115 in 2024). The escape route west was older still: from the early 1800s, New England whaling ships recruited crews in the islands, and by the mid-1800s New Bedford, Massachusetts became the anchor of Cape Verdean America, later supplemented by cranberry-bog labour in southeastern Massachusetts. Emigration accelerated after 1869 amid drought, starvation and economic decline; US restrictionist laws in 1922 choked it off; the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act reopened it. Independence arrived only in 1975, after the joint liberation struggle with Guinea-Bissau. The result: a nation whose defining infrastructure is the emigrant network itself.

raw_evidence.label: Morna and 'Sodade': the diaspora's soundtrack (UNESCO-listed)
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde's national music genre is literally about this story. Morna — voice, poetry, guitar and cavaquinho, sung in Cape Verdean Creole — was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 11 December 2019; UNESCO's own description lists its themes as love, departure, separation, reunion and longing. Its emotional core is 'sodade' (Creole for the Portuguese saudade): the mixture of nostalgia and sadness that grips both those who leave and those who stay. The genre's global face was Cesaria Evora (1941-2011), the 'Barefoot Diva' from Mindelo, whose signature song 'Sodade' — a lament addressed to an emigrant bound for Sao Tome, the very contract-labour route in det_12 — carried the emigrant's longing to world audiences, alongside 'Petit Pays', her ode to the small homeland. Morna is played wherever the diaspora lives — New England, Portugal, the Netherlands, France, West Africa. BGM guidance for the Scout/Designer: morna (ideally Cesaria Evora's 'Sodade' or a license-clean morna recording) is the tonally perfect BGM — a real recording, per the real-media policy; the UNESCO listing and the Sao Tome lyric connection make it load-bearing, not decorative.

raw_evidence.label: Morna and 'Sodade': the diaspora's soundtrack (UNESCO-listed)
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde's national music genre is literally about this story. Morna — voice, poetry, guitar and cavaquinho, sung in Cape Verdean Creole — was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 11 December 2019; UNESCO's own description lists its themes as love, departure, separation, reunion and longing. Its emotional core is 'sodade' (Creole for the Portuguese saudade): the mixture of nostalgia and sadness that grips both those who leave and those who stay. The genre's global face was Cesaria Evora (1941-2011), the 'Barefoot Diva' from Mindelo, whose signature song 'Sodade' — a lament addressed to an emigrant bound for Sao Tome, the very contract-labour route in det_12 — carried the emigrant's longing to world audiences, alongside 'Petit Pays', her ode to the small homeland. Morna is played wherever the diaspora lives — New England, Portugal, the Netherlands, France, West Africa. BGM guidance for the Scout/Designer: morna (ideally Cesaria Evora's 'Sodade' or a license-clean morna recording) is the tonally perfect BGM — a real recording, per the real-media policy; the UNESCO listing and the Sao Tome lyric connection make it load-bearing, not decorative.

raw_evidence.label: Sao Tome: the one big destination that is dying out
raw_evidence.content: Of 25 destinations, only five shrank between 1990 and 2024, and one dwarfs the rest: Sao Tome and Principe fell from 4,250 (the 3rd-largest community in 1990) to 1,115 (-73.8%), declining in every single wave. This is the demographic echo of the colonial contract-labour system that shipped ~80,000 Cape Verdeans to Sao Tome's cocoa plantations between 1900 and 1970 (det_12): the deportee generation is aging out and no new migration replaces it. The community that Cesaria Evora's 'Sodade' laments is literally disappearing from the table.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_03: Sao Tome and Principe, the one shrinking destination ---
print("=== ana_03 ===")
st = piv.loc["Sao Tome and Principe"]
print("Sao Tome and Principe wave series (year: migrants):")
for y, v in st.items():
    print(f"  {y}: {int(v):,}")
print(f"Change 1990->2024: {int(st[2024]) - int(st[1990]):,} ({(st[2024] / st[1990] - 1) * 100:.1f}%)")
shrunk = piv[piv[2024] < piv[1990]].index.tolist()
print(f"Destinations with 2024 < 1990 (of {len(piv)}): {shrunk}")
raw_evidence.output:

  1995: 3,343
  2000: 2,488
  2005: 1,956
  2010: 1,538
  2015: 1,363
  2020: 1,220
  2024: 1,115

raw_evidence.label: Remittances: from 28% of GDP to 12% — dependence receding as the economy grows
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's World Bank series shows personal remittances received were 28.2% of Cabo Verde's GDP in 1980, drifting down to 12.3% in 2024 — still among the highest shares in Sub-Saharan Africa (EUDiF's factsheet cites 13.5% of GDP, USD 313M inflow, in its December 2023 update). The right reading is NOT that the diaspora matters less: absolute inflows kept growing (a record 30%+ jump in 2021 alone, per The Conversation), remittances remain a bigger financial flow than foreign aid or FDI, and the declining share mostly reflects the denominator — GDP growth driven by tourism (~25% of GDP, enabling ~40% of all economic activity, per the US State Department's 2025 investment climate statement). For the analyst: the 1980-2024 remittance share series is the story's economic spine; consider pairing the declining share with World Bank absolute inflows, and rank Cabo Verde against other economies in the same WDI indicator (it sat among the world's most remittance-dependent economies through the 1980s-90s) rather than asserting a present-day global top rank.

raw_evidence.label: Remittances: 28.2% of GDP in 1980, 12.3% in 2024
raw_evidence.content: The World Bank series opens in 1980 with remittances worth 28.2% of Cabo Verde's GDP -- the series' all-time peak -- and closes 2024 at 12.3%. The arc is not a straight decline: an 18-19% plateau through the 1980s-90s (1990s mean 18.2%), a slide to the 7.2% low of 2010 as tourism-led GDP growth outpaced inflows, then a pandemic-era resurgence to 15.3% in 2021 (the diaspora sent MORE when tourism collapsed) before easing back. Dependence receded because the denominator grew (det_13), not because the diaspora stopped sending.

# --- ana_06: CPV remittance arc 1980-2024 ---
print("=== ana_06 ===")
first, last = cpv.iloc[0], cpv.iloc[-1]
peak = cpv.loc[cpv.remittances_pct_gdp.idxmax()]
low = cpv.loc[cpv.remittances_pct_gdp.idxmin()]
print(f"first: {int(first.year)} = {first.remittances_pct_gdp:.1f}% of GDP")
print(f"peak : {int(peak.year)} = {peak.remittances_pct_gdp:.1f}%")
print(f"low  : {int(low.year)} = {low.remittances_pct_gdp:.1f}%")
print(f"last : {int(last.year)} = {last.remittances_pct_gdp:.1f}%")
cpv["decade"] = (cpv.year // 10) * 10
dec = cpv.groupby("decade").remittances_pct_gdp.mean().round(1)
print("decade means (% of GDP):")
print(dec.to_string())
print("full series (year, pct):")
print(", ".join(f"{int(y)}:{v:.1f}" for y, v in zip(cpv.year, cpv.remittances_pct_gdp)))
