raw_evidence.label: Remittances: from 28% of GDP to 12% — dependence receding as the economy grows
raw_evidence.content: The dataset's World Bank series shows personal remittances received were 28.2% of Cabo Verde's GDP in 1980, drifting down to 12.3% in 2024 — still among the highest shares in Sub-Saharan Africa (EUDiF's factsheet cites 13.5% of GDP, USD 313M inflow, in its December 2023 update). The right reading is NOT that the diaspora matters less: absolute inflows kept growing (a record 30%+ jump in 2021 alone, per The Conversation), remittances remain a bigger financial flow than foreign aid or FDI, and the declining share mostly reflects the denominator — GDP growth driven by tourism (~25% of GDP, enabling ~40% of all economic activity, per the US State Department's 2025 investment climate statement). For the analyst: the 1980-2024 remittance share series is the story's economic spine; consider pairing the declining share with World Bank absolute inflows, and rank Cabo Verde against other economies in the same WDI indicator (it sat among the world's most remittance-dependent economies through the 1980s-90s) rather than asserting a present-day global top rank.

The rank then slid to #40 by 2010 as GDP grew, and has since stabilised in the high teens-to-twenties (#18 in 2024). The country's economic history 1980-2024 can be read off a single rank series.

# --- ana_08: Rank history 1980-2024 (best-ever global rank) ---

for y in range(1980, 2025):
    yy = rc[(rc.year == y)].dropna(subset=["remittances_pct_gdp"])
    yy = yy.sort_values("remittances_pct_gdp", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
    row = yy[yy["Country Code"] == "CPV"]
    if row.empty:
        continue
    rank = int(row.index[0]) + 1
    hist.append((y, rank, len(yy), round(row.iloc[0].remittances_pct_gdp, 1)))
h = pd.DataFrame(hist, columns=["year", "cpv_rank", "n_countries", "cpv_pct"])
print(h.to_string(index=False))
best = h.loc[h.cpv_rank.idxmin()]
top10_years = h[h.cpv_rank <= 10]
print(f"best-ever rank: #{int(best.cpv_rank)} of {int(best.n_countries)} in {int(best.year)} "
      f"({best.cpv_pct}% of GDP)")
print(f"years ranked in the global top 10: {len(top10_years)} "
      f"({', '.join(str(int(y)) for y in top10_years.year)})")

raw_evidence.label: The development miracle: 2nd country ever to graduate from LDC status
raw_evidence.content: The same country that lost a quarter of its people to famine within living memory is now one of Africa's most celebrated development stories — and the diaspora financed much of the climb. In December 2007 the UN graduated Cabo Verde from Least Developed Country status, only the SECOND country ever to achieve this (after Botswana in 1994; Maldives followed in 2011). Fifty years after independence it is an upper-middle-income state, ranks third on Africa's governance index, has the second-highest life expectancy in Africa (75-77 years) and among the continent's lowest child-mortality rates, and is regularly cited among Africa's most stable democracies. This is the 'why it matters' engine of the story: the diaspora is not a footnote to Cape Verde's development — remittances, return investment and now footballing talent are the mechanism of it.

raw_evidence.label: The Elo climb: world #138 in 1998 to #64 -- and an all-time peak mid-World Cup
raw_evidence.content: Running a standard Elo (K 60/50/40/30/20 by tournament, goal-difference multiplier, +100 home advantage, everyone starts at 1500 -- constants documented in code) over all 49,493 played internationals since 1872: Cape Verde's first recorded match is a 3-2 loss in Gambia in 1959 (one colonial-era friendly), the continuous record starts at the 1979 Amilcar Cabral Cup. The trajectory bottoms at 1383 (world #115) in 1988 and again 1384 (#138 of 198 FIFA-family teams) in 1998, then climbs almost monotonically for 25 years: #108 in 2010, #86 in 2014, #64 by July 2026. The all-time peak rating, 1702, was set DURING the World Cup on 2026-06-26 (after the 0-0 with Saudi Arabia); even after the Argentina defeat the rating (1699) sits within 3 points of the peak. This is the quantitative arc of det_02's 'small nation rising'.

            h, a = row.home_team, row.away_team
            rh, ra = R2.get(h, 1500.0), R2.get(a, 1500.0)
            adv = 0 if row.neutral else 100
            we_h = 1 / (10 ** (-((rh + adv) - ra) / 400) + 1)
            margin = abs(row.home_score - row.away_score)
            w_h = 1.0 if row.home_score > row.away_score else (0.0 if row.home_score < row.away_score else 0.5)
            delta = k_factor(row.tournament) * goal_mult(margin) * (w_h - we_h)
            R2[h], R2[a] = rh + delta, ra - delta
            N2[h] = N2.get(h, 0) + 1; N2[a] = N2.get(a, 0) + 1
            LAST2[h] = row.date; LAST2[a] = row.date
            idx += 1
        if CV not in R2:
            continue
        pool = {t: r for t, r in R2.items()
                if N2[t] >= 10 and LAST2[t] >= f"{y - 3}-01-01" and t in FIFA}
        rank = 1 + sum(r > R2[CV] for r in pool.values())
        yr_rows.append((y, round(R2[CV]), rank, len(pool)))
    print("year-end rating + world rank (established teams: >=10 matches, active <=4y):")
    print("year rating rank pool")
    for y, r_, rk_, np_ in yr_rows:
        print(f"{y} {r_} {rk_} {np_}")

    modern = cv[cv.date >= "1979"]

          f"{peak.away_team}, {peak.tournament})")
    print(f"rating after final data match ({cv.iloc[-1].date}): {cv.iloc[-1].cv_post:.0f}")

    year_marks = sorted(set(int(d[:4]) for d in cv.date if int(d[:4]) >= 1979))

    idx = 0

            row = dfi[idx]

            rh, ra = R2.get(h, 1500.0), R2.get(a, 1500.0)
            adv = 0 if row.neutral else 100
            we_h = 1 / (10 ** (-((rh + adv) - ra) / 400) + 1)
            margin = abs(row.home_score - row.away_score)
            w_h = 1.0 if row.home_score > row.away_score else (0.0 if row.home_score < row.away_score else 0.5)
            delta = k_factor(row.tournament) * goal_mult(margin) * (w_h - we_h)
            R2[h], R2[a] = rh + delta, ra - delta
            N2[h] = N2.get(h, 0) + 1; N2[a] = N2.get(a, 0) + 1
            LAST2[h] = row.date; LAST2[a] = row.date
            idx += 1

                if N2[t] >= 10 and LAST2[t] >= f"{y - 3}-01-01" and t in FIFA}
        rank = 1 + sum(r > R2[CV] for r in pool.values())

    print("year rating rank pool")

    e["gap"] = ((e.pre_away + 0) - (e.pre_home + adv)).where(home_won,
               (e.pre_home + adv) - (e.pre_away + 0))  # adjusted loser - winner
    e["w_score"] = e.home_score.where(home_won, e.away_score).astype(int)
    e["l_score"] = e.away_score.where(home_won, e.home_score).astype(int)

              f"{r_.w_score}-{r_.l_score} ({r_.tournament}) "
              f"gap {r_.gap:.0f} [{r_.w_pre:.0f} vs {r_.l_pre:.0f}]")
    cv_ups = e[(e.winner == CV) & (e.gap > 0)].sort_values("gap", ascending=False).head(5)
    print("Cape Verde's biggest Elo upsets:")

        print(f"  {r_.date} beat {r_.loser} {r_.w_score}-{r_.l_score} "
              f"({r_.tournament}) gap {r_.gap:.0f}")

          f"{len(e):,} decided matches: #{int((e.gap > pt_gap).sum()) + 1}")
    wc_ups = e[e.tournament == "FIFA World Cup"].sort_values("gap", ascending=False).head(5)
    print("biggest FIFA World Cup FINALS upsets by Elo gap:")
    for r_ in wc_ups.itertuples(index=False):

              f"gap {r_.gap:.0f}")
    last_wc = cv[cv.date == "2026-07-03"].iloc[0]
    arg_gap = last_wc.opp_pre - last_wc.cv_pre  # neutral venue, no adv
    n_bigger = int((e.gap > arg_gap).sum())
    n_bigger_wc = int((e[e.tournament == "FIFA World Cup"].gap > arg_gap).sum())

    cv_rank = [t for t, _ in board].index(CV) + 1
    print(f"current Elo (post {max(d for d in df.date)} data, FIFA-family teams): "

                       encoding="utf-8-sig")
    countries = set(meta[meta.Region.notna()]["Country Code"])
    p25 = pop[(pop.year == 2025) & (pop["Country Code"].isin(countries))]
    by_name = p25.set_index("Country Name").population
    TEAM_TO_WB = {
        "United States": "United States", "South Korea": "Korea, Rep.",
        "North Korea": "Korea, Dem. People's Rep.", "Iran": "Iran, Islamic Rep.",
        "Ivory Coast": "Cote d'Ivoire", "Egypt": "Egypt, Arab Rep.",
        "Turkey": "Turkiye", "Russia": "Russian Federation",
        "Czech Republic": "Czechia", "Venezuela": "Venezuela, RB",
        "DR Congo": "Congo, Dem. Rep.", "Republic of Ireland": "Ireland",
        "Cape Verde": "Cabo Verde", "Curaçao": "Curacao",
        "Slovakia": "Slovak Republic", "Syria": "Syrian Arab Republic",
        "Kyrgyzstan": "Kyrgyz Republic", "Gambia": "Gambia, The",
        "Congo": "Congo, Rep.", "Laos": "Lao PDR", "Vietnam": "Viet Nam",
    }
    print(f"Elo top {cv_rank} with 2025 population (n/a = no WB row, e.g. UK nations):")
    rows16 = []
    for i, (t, r_) in enumerate(board[:cv_rank], 1):
        wbn = TEAM_TO_WB.get(t, t)
        p_ = int(by_name[wbn]) if wbn in by_name.index else None
        rows16.append((i, t, round(r_), p_))
        print(f"  #{i} {t} {r_:.0f} pop={p_ if p_ is not None else 'n/a'}")
    above = [x for x in rows16 if x[3] is not None and x[0] < cv_rank]
    min_above = min(above, key=lambda x: x[3])
    print(f"smallest-population team ranked ABOVE Cape Verde: {min_above[1]} "
          f"(#{min_above[0]}, pop {min_above[3]:,}) -> Cape Verde is the "
          f"least-populous team in the world's Elo top {cv_rank}")
    cv_pop = int(by_name["Cabo Verde"])
    smaller_ranked = [(i, t, r_, p_) for i, (t, r_) in enumerate(board, 1)
                      if (lambda w: w in by_name.index and by_name[w] < cv_pop)
                      (TEAM_TO_WB.get(t, t))]
    nxt = smaller_ranked[0] if smaller_ranked else None
    if nxt:
        print(f"first team with a SMALLER population on the board: {nxt[1]} "
              f"at rank #{nxt[0]} (Elo {nxt[2]:.0f})")
    pop_sorted = p25.sort_values("population").reset_index(drop=True)
    cv_pop_rank = int(pop_sorted[pop_sorted["Country Code"] == "CPV"].index[0]) + 1
    print(f"population rank: Cabo Verde #{cv_pop_rank} smallest of {len(pop_sorted)} "
          f"WB countries (bottom {cv_pop_rank / len(pop_sorted) * 100:.0f}%)")

raw_evidence.label: The run: first-ever qualification (Oct 2025) and an unbeaten-in-90-minutes World Cup
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde qualified for a World Cup for the first time on 13 October 2025, beating Eswatini 3-0 in Praia to win their CAF qualifying group. At the 2026 tournament they were drawn into Group H with Spain, Uruguay and Saudi Arabia — and never lost a match in 90 minutes all tournament: 0-0 vs Spain (June 15), 2-2 vs Uruguay (June 21, goals from Kevin Pina and Helio Varela), 0-0 vs Saudi Arabia (June 26). Three draws and 3 points were enough to finish second in the group, making Cape Verde the smallest nation ever to reach the knockout stage of a FIFA World Cup. Their exit required the reigning champions, extra time, and an own goal. For the analyst: all of these matches are rows in international_results.csv (scores recorded at full-time/extra-time, no shootouts in these fixtures).

Had they beaten Argentina on 2026-07-03 (523-point gap), it would have ranked ~#25 all-time and #2 among World Cup FINALS upsets ever, behind only Cameroon-Brazil 2022 (gap 534) and ahead of Saudi Arabia-Argentina 2022 (446) and USA-England 1950 (429). They came within nine minutes of it.

Had they beaten Argentina on 2026-07-03 (523-point gap), it would have ranked ~#25 all-time and #2 among World Cup FINALS upsets ever, behind only Cameroon-Brazil 2022 (gap 534) and ahead of Saudi Arabia-Argentina 2022 (446) and USA-England 1950 (429). They came within nine minutes of it.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: second-smallest by area, THIRD-least-populated WC nation ever
raw_evidence.content: The 'smallest nation' claim needs precision, and the story brief's framing ('second-smallest after Iceland') is now outdated. When Cape Verde qualified in October 2025 it was the smallest country by land area (4,033 sq km) and the second-least-populated (just under 525,000, behind only Iceland 2018 at ~337,000) ever to reach a World Cup. But Curacao (444 sq km, ~156,000 people) qualified a month later, making Cape Verde the second-smallest by land area and the THIRD-least-populated nation at a World Cup. The claim Cape Verde does own outright: smallest nation ever to reach the KNOCKOUT stage (Curacao did not advance; Iceland exited their 2018 group). The analyst must verify the population ranking computationally against 04_population/API_SP.POP.TOTL (WB total population) joined to the list of WC debutants/participants by tournament year — and the story should say 'one of the smallest nations ever at a World Cup, and the smallest ever in the knockout rounds' rather than repeating the stale 'second-smallest' line.

Only three sub-1M nations have EVER played a World Cup, all since 2018, two of them in 2026 -- the tournament's 48-team expansion opened a door small nations are walking through. Next on the all-time list: Trinidad and Tobago 2006 (1.30M), Kuwait 1982 (1.66M).

sentences.summary: ana_18: Smallest nation ever in the knockouts -- by a factor of five (ranking, strong). Data: 01_diaspora/cape_verde_emigrants_by_destination.csv, 01_diaspora/undesa_ims_2024_destination_origin.xlsx, 02_remittances/remittances_pct_gdp_tidy.csv, 03_football/international_results.csv, 03_football/squad_2026.csv, 04_population/population_total_tidy.csv, 02_remittances/Metadata_Country_*.csv + 04_population/Metadata_Country_*.csv (aggregate filters). Built on det_02, det_03.

raw_evidence.label: Smallest nation ever in the knockouts -- by a factor of five
raw_evidence.content: Using the exact post-1962 rule that a team advanced past the first round iff it played a 4th match in the edition: Cape Verde (527,326) is the least-populous nation ever to do it, and it is not close -- the next-smallest advancer in World Cup history is Uruguay 1966 at 2,707,646, i.e. 5.1x larger. The two smaller participants never advanced (Curacao and Iceland both exited after 3 group games). Scale of the achievement in one line: the average WC2026 participant country has 47.2 million people (median 30.2M) -- 89 times Cape Verde -- and the biggest, the US, is 648 times larger. The det_02/det_03 claim 'smallest nation ever to reach the knockout stage' is computationally verified (with the NI-1982 caveat recorded in ana_caveat_06).
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_18: smallest nation to advance past the first round ---
print("=== ana_18 ===")
adv = d[d.advanced].sort_values("population").head(12).reset_index(drop=True)
adv.index += 1
print("12 least-populous teams ever to ADVANCE past the first round (1962-2026):")
print(adv.to_string())
cv_adv = adv[adv.team == "Cape Verde"]
nxt = adv.iloc[1]
print(f"Cape Verde ({cv.population:,}) is the SMALLEST ever to advance; next: "
      f"{nxt.team} {nxt.edition} ({nxt.population:,}) = "
      f"{nxt.population / cv.population:.1f}x larger")
ice = d[(d.team == "Iceland")]
cur = d[(d.team == "Curaçao")]
print(f"the two smaller participants never advanced: "
      f"Curaçao 2026 played {int(cur.iloc[0].matches)} matches (group exit), "
      f"Iceland 2018 played {int(ice.iloc[0].matches)} (group exit)")
p26 = d[d.edition == 2026]
print(f"WC2026 participants covered: {len(p26)}/48 (England, Scotland lack WB rows)")
print(f"WC2026 population mean {p26.population.mean():,.0f}, "
      f"median {p26.population.median():,.0f}")
print(f"Cape Verde vs mean participant: 1 : {p26.population.mean() / cv.population:.0f}; "
      f"vs median: 1 : {p26.population.median() / cv.population:.0f}")
big = p26.sort_values('population', ascending=False).iloc[0]
print(f"largest 2026 participant: {big.team} ({big.population:,}) = "
      f"{big.population / cv.population:.0f}x Cape Verde")

sentences.summary: det_10: The heritage layer, Netherlands: ~23,000 by CBS count, 90% around Rotterdam. Source: Cape Verdeans in the Netherlands — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Verdeans_in_the_Netherlands) Facts: CBS: approximately 23,150 people of Cape Verdean migration background in the Netherlands (2022); About 90% live in the Rotterdam metropolitan area; largest concentration in Delfshaven (~8.8% of the borough)

raw_evidence.label: The heritage layer, Netherlands: ~23,000 by CBS count, 90% around Rotterdam
raw_evidence.content: The Netherlands is the squad's biggest birthplace (6 of the 26 players) and hosts one of the most concentrated Cape Verdean communities anywhere. Statistics Netherlands (CBS) counted roughly 23,150 people of Cape Verdean migration background in 2022 — versus just 12,601 born-in-Cape-Verde migrants in the UN's 2019 stock, another clean demonstration of the migrant-stock vs heritage gap. About 90% live in the Rotterdam metropolitan area; in the borough of Delfshaven they are about 8.8% of the population, and community estimates for Rotterdam run to 20,000-30,000 — often described as the largest Cape Verdean community in any city outside the islands. The community's origin is maritime: young Cape Verdean men signed on as sailors on Dutch ships in the 1960s-70s and settled by the port. Half a century later, that settlement pattern is producing World Cup goal scorers.

raw_evidence.label: The heritage layer, Netherlands: ~23,000 by CBS count, 90% around Rotterdam
raw_evidence.content: The Netherlands is the squad's biggest birthplace (6 of the 26 players) and hosts one of the most concentrated Cape Verdean communities anywhere. Statistics Netherlands (CBS) counted roughly 23,150 people of Cape Verdean migration background in 2022 — versus just 12,601 born-in-Cape-Verde migrants in the UN's 2019 stock, another clean demonstration of the migrant-stock vs heritage gap. About 90% live in the Rotterdam metropolitan area; in the borough of Delfshaven they are about 8.8% of the population, and community estimates for Rotterdam run to 20,000-30,000 — often described as the largest Cape Verdean community in any city outside the islands. The community's origin is maritime: young Cape Verdean men signed on as sailors on Dutch ships in the 1960s-70s and settled by the port. Half a century later, that settlement pattern is producing World Cup goal scorers.

raw_evidence.label: Morna and 'Sodade': the diaspora's soundtrack (UNESCO-listed)
raw_evidence.content: Cape Verde's national music genre is literally about this story. Morna — voice, poetry, guitar and cavaquinho, sung in Cape Verdean Creole — was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 11 December 2019; UNESCO's own description lists its themes as love, departure, separation, reunion and longing. Its emotional core is 'sodade' (Creole for the Portuguese saudade): the mixture of nostalgia and sadness that grips both those who leave and those who stay. The genre's global face was Cesaria Evora (1941-2011), the 'Barefoot Diva' from Mindelo, whose signature song 'Sodade' — a lament addressed to an emigrant bound for Sao Tome, the very contract-labour route in det_12 — carried the emigrant's longing to world audiences, alongside 'Petit Pays', her ode to the small homeland. Morna is played wherever the diaspora lives — New England, Portugal, the Netherlands, France, West Africa. BGM guidance for the Scout/Designer: morna (ideally Cesaria Evora's 'Sodade' or a license-clean morna recording) is the tonally perfect BGM — a real recording, per the real-media policy; the UNESCO listing and the Sao Tome lyric connection make it load-bearing, not decorative.

raw_evidence.label: The development miracle: 2nd country ever to graduate from LDC status
raw_evidence.content: The same country that lost a quarter of its people to famine within living memory is now one of Africa's most celebrated development stories — and the diaspora financed much of the climb. In December 2007 the UN graduated Cabo Verde from Least Developed Country status, only the SECOND country ever to achieve this (after Botswana in 1994; Maldives followed in 2011). Fifty years after independence it is an upper-middle-income state, ranks third on Africa's governance index, has the second-highest life expectancy in Africa (75-77 years) and among the continent's lowest child-mortality rates, and is regularly cited among Africa's most stable democracies. This is the 'why it matters' engine of the story: the diaspora is not a footnote to Cape Verde's development — remittances, return investment and now footballing talent are the mechanism of it.
